paras: The lynching of Blutcher Higgins and Dan Callicut took place in Corinth, Alcorn County, Mississippi, on the night of August 27–28, 1920, when a mob of 75 to 100 men forced the jailer to surrender his keys and hanged the two Black prisoners from a telegraph pole. The men, escaped chain-gang prisoners who had surrendered, were accused of striking down a guard. The county prosecuting attorney declared that "at least one" was innocent, and the guard was reported to have said neither had attacked him, a report his son disputed.

According to an Associated Press dispatch, Higgins and Callicut escaped from the county chain gang with two other prisoners after a guard, James Whitehurst, was knocked on the head. The two returned and surrendered to the sheriff, a third escapee was recaptured, and a fourth, named by the Memphis News Scimitar as George York, remained at large. Reports of Whitehurst's condition ranged from "not expected to live" to a certain recovery.

The AP placed the lynching early on August 28 and the Washington Times "late Friday night," while a syndicated Mississippi account said the mob assembled on a country road "August 29 at midnight." In that account, jailer J. D. King was called to the door, where one man demanded the keys to the cells at revolver point, and King complied. The mob took Higgins and Callicut from their cells, hanged them and dispersed quietly; early risers found the bodies at daybreak.

The AP put the pole near the jail, while the Mississippi account placed the hanging at the crossing of the Illinois Central and Southern railroads on the outskirts of town. Estimates of the mob ranged from 75 to 100 men in the AP story and one hundred masked men in a Jackson dispatch to twenty-five in the Chicago Defender.

King telephoned Sheriff Gray, who called County Attorney Thomas H. Johnston, and the two searched for the mob without finding any trace of it. Johnston said the mob "beyond question has killed at least one innocent negro" and promised "the most vigorous prosecution" if he could obtain evidence. A coroner's jury heard Sheriff Gray and jail inmates and adjourned; no report of a verdict, arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

On Sunday night, August 29, a mass meeting at the First Baptist church passed resolutions condemning the hanging as "a ruthless and inexcussable disregard of the courts of our country" and pledging aid to the officers.

White papers nationwide ran the wire story on August 29 and 30 under headlines such as "Two Negroes Lynched For Striking Down Guard," giving the assault as "alleged." The Norwich Bulletin's editorial "Where Lynching Is Winked At" argued that no crime meriting death had been committed. In Mississippi, the Southern Herald and the Macon Beacon headlined the guard's beating as "the cause," and the North Mississippi Herald reprinted the guard's denial under "Mob Is Condemned."

Black weeklies took up the story from September 3 and framed it as typical of the state, with headlines such as "Mississippi Crackers Snuff Out Life Of Convicts" in the Baltimore Afro-American and "Mississippi Keeps True to Her Form" in the Cleveland Advocate. An Associated Negro Press item ran as "Mississippi Cannibals Lynch Two Negroes," and the Afro-American printed Lucian B. Watkins's poem "White Wolves" with the Corinth news item as its epigraph. The Chicago Defender alleged that the mob's members were known to the jailer and officers and tied the lynching to Black residents leaving the area. The Negro Star reprinted a New Orleans Item editorial, "Corinth's Shame," which mocked the "orderly lynching," and the Metropolis Weekly Gazette headlined the guard's statement "Mississippi Mob Lynches Wrong Men For Assault."

The Memphis News Scimitar reported that Whitehurst declared neither hanged man was implicated and named George York as his assailant. Two days later the same paper quoted the guard's son, who said his father had named Callicutt as calling out to distract him while Higgins struck him with a shovel. An Associated Negro Press item in the Black Dispatch described the men as "accused of murdering a woman," a charge that appears in no other report.

bases: A mob of 75 to 100 men took two Black prisoners from the Alcorn County jail and hanged them (A3, A17, A2).

A mob numbering 75 to 100 forced the jailer to give up his keys and hanged two prisoners accused of assaulting a chain-gang guard, without any legal process (A3, A17); officials called it a mob act and sought the perpetrators (A17, A12).

The AP dispatch (A3), the Memphis News Scimitar special (A12) and the syndicated Mississippi account (A17) agree on the seizure and hanging of the two men; only whether the men had attacked the guard is disputed (A12, A14).

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Two Negroes Lynched For Striking Down Guard' and 'LYNCH 2 NEGROES IN CORINTH, MISS.' with the accusation given as alleged.
Norwich Bulletin editorial 'Where Lynching Is Winked At' called the men 'ruthlessly murdered'.
Mississippi papers headlined the guard's beating as 'the cause' but quoted Johnston calling it a 'fearful smirch' on the county.
Memphis News Scimitar: 'Corinth Mob Is Condemned by Alcorn Citizens'; a follow-up disputed the innocence report.
'Mississippi Crackers Snuff Out Life Of Convicts', 'Mississippi Keeps True to Her Form', 'Mississippi Cannibals Lynch Two Negroes', 'Mississippi Mob Lynches Wrong Men For Assault'.
Negro Star reprinted the New Orleans Item's 'Corinth's Shame'; the Afro-American printed the poem 'White Wolves'.

conflicts.note: The Aug. 28 AP dateline makes the night of Aug. 27-28 the best-supported date; the syndicated 'August 29' is inconsistent with the dated dispatches.
